subject: Abacus
hook: ABACUS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK
angle: ABACUS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK – its name doesn’t mean a dust‑covered board; it actually derives from the ancient Greek ἄβαξ meaning ‘a board without a base’
angle_support: The Latin word is derived from ancient Greek ἄβαξ (abax) which means something without a base, and colloquially, any piece of rectangular material.
While the table strewn with dust definition is popular, some argue evidence is insufficient for that conclusion.
title: The True Origin of the Abacus
description: We explore the etymology of the abacus, overturning the common myth that its name relates to a dust-strewn surface. Discover its actual Greek roots.
narration: ABACUS IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK You picture a dusty frame filled with beads used for ancient math. You assume the name implies a surface for dust. It was closer to something else. The term actually originates from the ancient Greek word abax. It literally translates to a board without a base. It described a flat, rectangular slab used for calculations, long before beads were ever added to the design. It was never about the dust; it was about the void.
